prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The untrained trace shows that the world does not behave as described: every action's column is shifted by +4 with wraparound. Examples: 1x1 at col 2 filled col 6, 1x2 at col 6 filled cols 2-3, and 1x2 at col 7 filled cols 3-4. Rows and brick shapes are unchanged. The starting network is translation-equivariant and its receptive field reaches only 2 cells. Its logit at anchor x can therefore never see the cells that the placement actually fills. Every placement looks like noise with negative expected reward, so the policy collapses to DONE (100% immediate DONE, score 0). The main fix is a learned position remap between cell space and action space, not a hard-coded shift, so the network can still work on other grid sizes or with other remaps. Pooling over footprints should use circular padding to cover the wraparound. A higher entropy bonus might also help to stop early collapse to DONE.

### Round 2
The traces show what is wrong with this world. Every placement lands 4 columns to the right of its anchor, wrapping around (X/2), while rows are unchanged. The observation itself is not shifted. The legality mask is computed from where the brick actually lands, so the shift is just a relabelling of actions, and a remap plus circular footprint pooling can represent it exactly. All six seeds scored 0, so nothing stands out from seed noise yet. Still, r1c3 (remap with entropy 0.03) is the only run that placed bricks at all. When it did, about 87% of the cells it filled were in the target (0.39 inside vs 0.06 outside per episode), so it did learn the remap. The real failure is ending the episode with DONE too early. Random placements earn negative reward, so DONE (reward 0) wins within the first 25% of training, before placement skill develops. This round tests anti-collapse fixes on r1c3 in a factorial design: a negative initial DONE bias, a more exploratory recipe, and both together.

### Round 3
Every trial scored 0 on both seeds. The traces show the world places action column x at actual column (x+4) mod 8, and rows are unchanged. The starting network can only see about 2 cells either side, so it cannot learn a 4-column offset. It falls back to DONE (reward 0) instead of random placements (about −0.18 each). The 8x8 remapping layers can represent the shift, but each column must learn its own source position, so learning is slow. r2c3 (DONE bias −3, entropy 0.05, 2 PPO epochs) is the only trial with signs of learning: immediate DONE fell to 49%, and its trace shows two correct shifted 1x1 placements. So the exploration recipe helps, and the bottleneck is learning the shift quickly. A layer that applies the same weights at every position and wraps around the edges, spanning the whole axis with one filter per channel, learns one shift shared by all positions. That should be far quicker and costs almost nothing in compute.

### Round 4
The world shifts every placement 4 columns, wrapping around the grid. Learned layers that span each whole axis and wrap at the edges (CircMix) learn this shift, and they turned 0.000 into r3c1 0.243 and r3c2 0.329. Seed spread within a trial is ±0.12, so where the mix sits (trunk or head) is not separated. Starting the DONE bias at -3, ent_coef 0.05 and 2 PPO epochs avoided the early collapse, though r3c2 came close (mean episode length 2.5 at 25% of training). One epoch gave 0: the agent never learned to stop and always ran to the 33-placement limit. r3c2's training success was still rising at the end (0.17 then 0.22), so the agent is short of updates or of signal, not stuck. In the traces, misses come from brick order and overhangs: bricks placed at layer 0 under target cells that should overhang, and stopping early with one column short. That points to (a) more credit for the end-of-episode exact-build bonus, (b) more gradient updates for the same samples, and (c) more head capacity to match the landing layer against the missing layer. Each candidate below makes one change to r3c2.

## Trial it ended with
name: circ head + 2x more updates
hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r3c2, except n_envs 128 and n_minibatches 16. Minibatches stay at 128 samples, and the total number of samples is unchanged. That gives twice as many PPO updates, and twice the learning-rate decay steps, on the same data. r3c2's training success was still climbing at the end, which suggests too few updates rather than too little data. Refuted if dev success is at or below 0.33, or if it collapses to DONE.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
